14870-rebuilding-britain-a-survey-of-pro:
Sir Alfred Hopkinson's 1918 survey asks how Britain should rebuild after the First World War. Its five parts run from aspirations and foundations through peace, retrenchment and reform to the goal, with chapters that still read as a programme.

International peace brings the League of Nations: need, scheme, conditions, scope and aim, with conclusions on victory and peace. Political peace covers constitution and democracy, industrial peace covers councils, hours and wages, and religious peace covers cooperation. State spending and income follow. Hopkinson writes as a practical reformer, seeking a settlement that would hold after victory.
24541-between-the-lines-secret-service-s:
Brevet Major H. B. Smith wrote these secret-service stories fifty years after the Civil War, recalling his work as a detective and provost marshal. His files open with the Harry Gilmor sword, move to New York Harbor forts in 1861 and 1862, and follow him to Fort McHenry, Harper's Ferry, and Johnson's Island.

Later files cover the draft riots of July 1863, the Knights of the Golden Circle, the Sons of Liberty, and a Copperhead plot for a northwestern confederacy. Smith tells his tales with humour and detail, naming generals, prisoners, and plotters. Readers get a firsthand view of the war's hidden front, where spies, guards, and detectives did their work.
29711-another-sheaf:
John Galsworthy's Another Sheaf, printed in 1919 by Charles Scribner's Sons of New York, gathers essays and sketches from the war years. Its contents run from The Road and The Sacred Work through a balance sheet of the soldier-workman and a children's jewel fund. France in 1916 and 1917, Englishman and Russian, American and Briton, and Anglo-American drama follow. The land in 1917 and 1918 closes the book.

Galsworthy writes with the humane, observant eye of a novelist turned essayist, weighing war, work, and nation. A voice in dripping stillness, with tramping of weary feet, opens one piece. Readers of Galsworthy and of wartime essays will find a thoughtful, civilized sheaf from a writer at his most public.
35903-rose-leaf-and-apple-leaf:
Rose Leaf and Apple Leaf is a book of verse by Rennell Rodd. Thomas Mosher printed the book for the poet at Portland, Maine, in 1906. Oscar Wilde wrote the opening piece, called L'Envoi, for the young poet. Sonnets, songs, and place poems fill the slim volume of verse. Titles run from From the Hill of Gardens to By the South Sea.

In the Coliseum, the Sea-King's Grave, and a Roman Mirror stand early. Sonnets bear names like Actea and Imperator Augustus in the Latin style. Songs include Long After and Where the Rhone Goes Down to the Sea. Atalanta, the Daisy, and pieces after Heine crowd the later pages. In Chartres Cathedral and Requiescat close the list of his poems. Wilde calls Rodd's love of art flawless and fervent in the envoi. Verses of sweet sadness and joy, he says, he brought to America.
39912-tom-willoughby-s-scouts-a-story-of:
Herbert Strang wrote a boys' tale of the war in German East Africa. Humphrey Milford and Oxford University Press issued Tom Willoughby's Scouts in 1919. Pictures by Wal Paget show Reinecke flinging up his arm. Twenty-one chapters run from Tanganyika to a raised siege at the close.

Passengers board the Hedwig von Wissmann at Kigoma on Lake Tanganyika in June 1914. Tom, Mwesa, and the foe Reinecke drive a tale of traps and trails. A deserter, a German offer, and a good haul crowd the middle parts. Boys gain a brisk war tale from a far, hard campaign.
40579-memoir-of-hendrick-zwaardecroon-co:
Hendrick Zwaardecroon, Commandeur of Jaffnapatam in Dutch Ceylon, wrote this memoir in 1697 to guide his council while he traveled to the Malabar Coast. Sophia Pieters translated it from the Dutch. The government printer at Colombo published the translation in 1911, with an introduction and notes by the government archivist. Zwaardecroon later became Governor-General of the Netherlands Indies.

He never returned to his post, and his memoir became a standing authority. Dutch officials quoted it through nearly the whole period of Dutch rule in Ceylon. The introduction praises its light on native industries, revenue sources, and the condition of the people. Old local terms are explained here for the first time. Its maps and place notes, the editor adds, are full and exact.
40838-the-empire-makers-a-romance-of-adv:
Hume Nesbit wrote this adventure novel of South Africa, in an edition dated 1900. His preface tells the shape of the tale at once. Three young men go out to South Africa, fall into trouble with the Transvaal government, and then find an ancient nation hidden in Central Africa. On their return they take a small part in the war then raging.

Nesbit writes as a firm friend of the British Empire, and his preface says so in strong terms. He praises the empire and attacks the Boer leaders without pause. The romance mixes lost peoples, danger, and battle. It also stands as a clear record of how many British readers saw the South African War at the time.
56222-bertha-s-christmas-vision-an-autum:
Bertha's Christmas Vision is the first book of Horatio Alger, issued at Boston in 1856. Its subtitle calls it an autumn sheaf. Brown, Bazin and Company published it. Alger dedicated the book to his mother. Her sympathy kept much from staying unwritten, he says. Names like Little Charlie and Little Floy fill the dedication. A Browning poem on weeping children is quoted there.

The sheaf gathers tales and sketches of child life. Bertha, with her precious gifts, is its central child. The Child of the Street is another of its figures. Alger later won fame with tales of bootblacks and newsboys. Ragged Dick made his name a byword for rising boys. This first volume shows the seed of that career. Its tone is tender where the later books are brisk. It stands as a young minister's offering.
57778-a-sheaf:
A Sheaf is a gathering of the prose of John Galsworthy. It came out in London in 1916 from William Heinemann, and is given to William Archer. The author's note states what the book is. The volume is but a gleaning of non-creative writings, it says, mostly pleas of one sort or other.

The novelist calls them the wild oats of a novelist, bound up at the request of others. He had no wanton joy in sowing them, he says. He adds a point of fact: he has not, in his own person, gained a penny by anything in the volume, nor will he gain by what comes from it later. The note thus sets the tone of the book: a set of public pleas and essays by a famed writer, put out without profit to him.
68747-incwadi-yami-or-twenty-years-perso:
Matthews, a doctor, wrote Incwadi Yami, or Twenty Years' Personal Experience in South Africa, printed in London in 1887. Incwadi yami is Zulu for my book. Portraits of the Cape's great men front it: Rose Innes, Villiers, and the Kimberley members among them. Matthews had been vice-president of the legislative council and senior member for Kimberley.

He gives the notes to his fellow colonists, and above all to his friends on the diamond fields, who twice returned him at the head of the poll. District surgeon days, a practice at Verulam, and the rush to the diamond diggings fill the early tale. Students of South Africa get a full insider's twenty years.
71867-the-leaf:
Leaf is a story by Robert F Young, from a magazine called Infinity dated March nineteen fifty eight. Pictures by Richard Kluga go with it. Its headnote says that even a desperate present could not spoil the hero's memories of other days in the woods. One such day was a lazy one when he shot eleven squirrels, it recalls.

The tale opens on just such a memory, from several years back. In mid autumn the last red leaves were fluttering down. The hunter took his rifle into the hickory woods and settled against a shaggy trunk. He waited with the gun across his knees. A red squirrel came out on a high limb and posed there. It sat still as if painted against bare branches and a milk blue sky. He raised the rifle slowly, in no hurry.
78062-the-flower-and-the-leaf:
The Flower and the Leaf is a Middle English poem in rhyme royal, long ascribed to Chaucer circle, here printed with leaf decorated initials. The poem opens in spring. When Phoebus had whirled his chair of gold up the starry sky and entered the Bull, sweet showers descended soft, it begins. The ground gave many a wholesome air, and every plain was clothed fair. Small flowers spring in field and meadow.

The teller, glad of the season, lay one night unable to sleep though free of sickness or disease. Up he rose three hours after twelve, about the springing of the day. He put on his gear and passed to a pleasant grove before sunrise. Great oaks straight as a line stood there, with grass fresh of hue below. A debate of flower and leaf parties follows in the dream. Poetry readers get a fifteenth century allegory in old spelling.
9596-reform-and-politics-part-2-from-the:
Part two of Whittier's Reform and Politics gathers his essays on reform causes of his age. Utopian Schemes and Political Theorists opens, chiding conservatives who fear all change as a threat to order. Later essays take up woman suffrage, Italian unity, Indian civilization, and reading for the blind. The Indian question, the Republican Party, and international arbitration follow.

Whittier argues as a Quaker reformer: change may be slow, but justice cannot wait on comfort. His prose stays plain and earnest, aimed at citizens, not scholars. A reader gets a clear view of a reformer's mind, applied to votes for women, peace, and the rights of native peoples.
britannica-1911-bonde-gustaf:
Gustaf Bonde (1620–1667), a Swedish count and statesman, stood out for preaching peace in a war-hungry age. While other Swedish politicians reached for war on slight pretexts, Bonde opposed even Charles X's popular Polish campaign. Once war was decided, though, he helped the king find the money to fight it.

He backed strict economy and the taking back of crown lands that had passed to nobles, and in 1655 he sat on the land-recovery commission. He became lord high treasurer in 1659 and a regent during Charles XI's childhood. His plan of 1661 aimed to free Sweden from foreign subsidies by peace, thrift, trade growth, and more land recovery. His budget of the next year later guided Charles XI, the entry notes.
britannica-1911-leaf:
Leaf is a botany article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the green flat organs borne on the stem of a plant. In plain speech the word covers all such growths. It is also lent to like things: a thin sheet of metal, the hinged flap of a table, or the page of a book.

Study has shown that many plant parts that look unlike leaves are their true matches in build. The scales of a bulb are such parts, and so are the parts of a flower. Men once called these changed or transformed leaves. That phrase, the article says, can mislead. All parts built on the leaf plan now go under one name, phyllome, or leaf-structure. The entry then sets out the leaf's forms with plates and terms.
britannica-1911-lindstrom-gustaf:
Gustaf Lindstrom was a Swedish student of fossils who lived from eighteen twenty-nine to nineteen one. He was born at Wisby on the isle of Gotland. He took his degree at Uppsala and then turned to the life of the Baltic Sea. Work as a school teacher left him time for deep study.

His spare hours went to the old rocks of Gotland and the shells and beasts held in them. He wrote on corals, shell fish, and the great sea beasts of that age. He also fixed the true nature of one odd coral. In time he took charge of the state store of fossils at Stockholm.
britannica-1911-whittier-john-greenleaf:
John Greenleaf Whittier is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, which calls him the Quaker poet of freedom and faith. He was born in a farmhouse in the Merrimack Valley at Haverhill, in the state of Massachusetts, on the seventeenth of December 1807. He died in 1892. The hosted text reaches his article after the tail of the entry before it.

The article roots his verse in his family and his faith. His forebear Thomas Whittier had fought for fair treatment of Quakers in New England. The poet held to the Quaker faith, its dress, and its speech all his life. His father was a farmer of small means and free spirit. The text notes his frail frame, his shyness, and his schooling at a plain district school.
rebuilding-britain-a-survey-of-problems-:
Sir Alfred Hopkinson, K.C., surveyed how Britain might rebuild after the World War in a book Cassell issued in 1918. His plan starts with the course of the war years and their hopes and foundations. The rest of the book is grouped under one word: peace, in four kinds.

For peace between nations he gives five chapters to a League of Nations, its need, scheme, conditions, scope, and aim. Political peace turns on the constitution and democracy at home. Industrial peace covers councils, long hours, and wages. A fourth part, on religious peace, begins as the contents break off, showing the breadth of his rebuilding plan.
reform-and-politics-part-2-from-the-work:
John Greenleaf Whittier's essays on reform and politics are gathered in this part of his works, opening with a study of utopian schemes and political theorists. Whittier there describes men whose settled ease makes them fear any change in the state. They hold the evils of the old order to be fixed in fallible human nature.

Such men, he writes, enjoy the good of their own lot and look with calm unconcern on evils that strike only their neighbors. Later pieces take up woman suffrage, Italian unity, Indian civilization, reading for the blind, and international arbitration. The Republican Party and our dumb relations also draw the poet-reformer's pen.
